knowledge_type_note: Official rule. The permanent-vs-temporary distinction is explicit in the Laws.
definition_short: A single move of king and rook: the king moves two squares towards the rook, and that rook jumps to the square the king crossed.
definition_long:
FIDE Art. 3.8.2: 'a move of the king and either rook of the same colour along the player's first rank, counting as a single move of the king and executed as follows: the king is transferred from its original square two squares towards the rook on its original square, then that rook is transferred to the square the king has just crossed.'

Art. 3.8.2.1 — the right is LOST permanently if the king has already moved, or with a rook that has already moved. Art. 3.8.2.2 — castling is prevented TEMPORARILY if the king's square, the square it crosses, or the square it lands on is attacked, or if any piece stands between king and rook.

The lost/prevented distinction is the part implementations most often get wrong. Moving the king and returning it does not restore the right; a check that passes does restore the possibility.

history.notes: Historical development of castling not yet researched for this record.

preconditions: King and the chosen rook are both on their original squares and neither has moved
The king is not in check, does not cross an attacked square, and does not land on one
indicators_for: Castling rights flag still set for that side and that rook
indicators_against: King or that rook has moved at any earlier point
The crossed or destination square is attacked

exceptions: The ROOK may be attacked, and in queenside castling the b1/b8 square the rook crosses may be attacked — only the king's three squares matter.
Rights once lost never return, even if the piece goes back to its original square.
limitations: Affects position identity for repetition: Art. 9.2.3.2 — positions are not the same if a king had castling rights with a rook that has not moved but forfeited them after moving.
Reported for the MOVE, not for the rights. Almost every opening position has castling rights, and a concept true of almost every position is not news; a king moving two squares is.

examples.note: both castling moves are legally available to the side to move. This is a DEFINITIONAL example: the feature is present by the rules of chess and by the page's own move generator, which is the whole of what needs verifying. No engine was consulted, because no engine is needed to establish that a legal move exists. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

by_level.beginner: Castling moves your king two squares towards a rook and hops that rook over to the other side — it tucks the king away and brings the rook into play in one move.
by_level.intermediate: Castling is legal only if neither piece has moved, the squares between are empty, and the king is not in, through, or into check. Note the rook may be attacked.
by_level.advanced: Art. 3.8.2. Distinguish rights lost permanently (3.8.2.1) from castling prevented temporarily (3.8.2.2); the latter can be restored.
